transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Gupta (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (CTO, LumosPay), Aisha Khan (Lead ML Engineer), Ben Harper (SRE)

Summary:
- Quick intro and discovery on latency/throughput needs for fraud detection model (short prompts and some longer context).
- Discussed p95 targets, concurrency, streaming vs non-streaming, token/sec benchmarking, and deployment options (Hosted/Dedicated/Private).
- Agreed to share sample prompts and run token/sec benchmarks; Redwood to send security docs and pricing; follow-up demo for Private infra next week.

Topics:
- p95 latency targets (numbers around 150-200ms)
- concurrency: 40-80 concurrent streaming requests
- streaming performance and token/sec (3k-5k tokens/sec target for peak batch scoring)
- dedicated capacity pricing and pilot scope
- security: SOC2, KMS, VPC, audit logs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Meyers: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros — i'm jordan, ae for redwood, and with me is priya our se.
[00:06] Carlos Ruiz: hi, carlos here, cto at lumospay, got a few people from infra and ml — aisha and ben on the call.
[00:12] Aisha Khan: hey all, aisha, lead ml eng.
[00:14] Ben Harper: ben, sre focusing on latency and ops.
[00:18] Jordan Meyers: awesome, thanks. high-level — we want to understand your latency and throughput SLOs, current infra, and what success looks like. can you walk us through the use case?
[00:26] Carlos Ruiz: sure, so we do real-time fraud scoring at authorization time. most prompts are short, like 50-150 tokens summarizing transaction and user signals, but we also have a batch scoring pipeline for nightly risk models with larger contexts. the critical piece is authorizations — we need p95 well under 200ms ideally, because anything slower impacts merchant checkout.
[00:44] Jordan Meyers: okay p95 under 200ms for auth path, got it. is that for single-token generation or full responses? are you streaming responses to the client?
[00:53] Aisha Khan: we stream the decision to our gateway, yes. typical response size is small, a couple of tokens, but we do rely on streaming so the server-side tail matters. concurrency on peak — roughly 40 to 80 concurrent auth requests.
[01:07] Priya Gupta: okay, so streaming + concurrency. are you measuring in p95 token latency or p95 response latency? sometimes folks say p95 but it's per-token p95 which can differ.
[01:16] Ben Harper: right now we instrument response latency at the gateway, so it captures network + model. for us p95 response end-to-end is the metric we care about.
[01:23] Priya Gupta: perfect, that helps. given that, we usually look at three levers: routing & model variant (hosted vs dedicated vs private), batching and KV/prefix cache, and quantization/ops. for streaming we optimize the runtime to keep token emission latency low — continuous batching can help throughput but hurts tail latency if not tuned.
[01:38] Carlos Ruiz: what's the delta between hosted api and dedicated for this kind of workload? we need predictable tail behavior, not spikes.
[01:44] Jordan Meyers: great question. hosted can be the fastest to get going — lower setup time — but with noisy noisy multi-tenant contention tails can be higher during bursts. dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and consistent throughput; you can set autoscale and burst policies. private (vpc/on-prem) gives max isolation but has setup overhead. we see customers hitting stable p95s ~120-180ms on dedicated for small responses at 50 concurrency for optimized models.
[02:08] Aisha Khan: that 120-180ms number — is that token emission p95 or full response at our network?
[02:13] Priya Gupta: that's model-side p95 for the full response emission on our runtime, excluding customer network egress. end-to-end you'll add 10-40ms depending on region and proximity.
[02:22] Ben Harper: do you support prefix/KV cache so repeated sessions are faster? a lot of our flows have repeated context.
[02:27] Priya Gupta: yes, we support KV cache and prefix caching. it materially improves p50 and p95 for repeated prefixes — we typically see 2-5x token/sec improvements for hot prefixes. for fraud, if you have a canonical prompt shape it's low-hanging fruit.
[02:40] Carlos Ruiz: ok interesting. another thing — our batch scoring needs to do 3k to 5k tokens/sec sustained for some models. is that per node or cluster aggregate?
[02:49] Jordan Meyers: depends on hardware and quantization. on A100-like nodes with optimized kernels you can hit high tokens/sec per GPU for FP16/4-bit quantized variants. for example, a single ded-sku optimized for throughput could do ~2k-3k tokens/sec for heavy decoders; with batching across multiple GPUs you can scale linearly. we'll confirm exact numbers in the benchmark template.
[03:07] Aisha Khan: do you do token/sec benchmarking for customer prompts or just synthetic? we need realistic numbers.
[03:11] Priya Gupta: we prefer customer prompt sets — synthetic benchmarks can mislead. we'll run the token/sec/latency bench with your prompts and sequence length distribution. i'll need a sample prompt set and typical concurrency profile.
[03:21] Carlos Ruiz: we can share prompt samples, but can you guarantee the p95 target?
[03:25] Jordan Meyers: we can't guarantee without running the benchmarks, but historically with dedicated pools customers hit their p95s with the right kernel/quantization and batching configs. we'll do a pilot where we run end-to-end benchmarks and tune configs.
[03:37] Ben Harper: security — SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs — do you have those for hosted?
[03:43] Jordan Meyers: yes, hosted is SOC2 compliant; we have SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and integrate with customer KMS for Private and Dedicated options. our private offering supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering for audit requirements.
[03:58] Aisha Khan: latency-wise, how much does VPC peering or on-prem add? our infra team is sensitive to cross-region hops.
[04:04] Priya Gupta: if you co-locate or use private deployment in-region, network latency is minimal — typical extra is 5-20ms depending on topology. the biggest variability is model runtime tail behavior, not the network if it's in the same AZ.
[04:17] Carlos Ruiz: on pricing — predictable monthly for dedicated is important because we want capacity planning. do you have pilot pricing?
[04:23] Jordan Meyers: yes, we provide pilot reserved capacity with a short-term commit to validate throughput and latency. we'll follow up with a pricing estimate for the pilot and a longer-term committed tier.
[04:33] Aisha Khan: curious about streaming overhead — do you see higher p95 when streaming compared to non-streaming?
[04:39] Priya Gupta: streaming can surface tail variability because tokens are emitted incrementally. our runtime optimizes for low per-token emission latency; we also have fallback policies to emit more aggressively under load. it's a tradeoff, but we've tuned it for common conversational workloads — should translate to your short response sizes.
[04:54] Ben Harper: what about model variants — smaller quantized models vs larger ones — how do you recommend?
[04:59] Priya Gupta: if accuracy requirements allow, quantized variants (4-bit or int8) give big throughput gains and lower latency. we can run evaluation on your dev set to measure regression. for auth decisions if model size can be reduced without hurting precision, we typically recommend a quantized medium model on Dedicated for stable tails.
[05:18] Carlos Ruiz: ok that's helpful. next steps?
[05:20] Jordan Meyers: action items: priya will run token/sec/lateny benchmarks with your prompts; carlos to share prompt set and concurrency profile; i'll send SOC2 and security docs plus pilot pricing. we'll schedule a private deployment deep-dive with your infra team next wednesday if that works.
[05:33] Aisha Khan: next wed works for us. i'll loop in our infra folks.
[05:36] Ben Harper: thanks, please include specifics about KMS integration and audit log retention.
[05:40] Jordan Meyers: will do. thanks everyone.
[05:43] Carlos Ruiz: thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription quality: some product names auto-transcribed (e.g., "Redwood Dedicated" appeared once as "Redwood Decadent" in internal notes), minor word swaps in technical terms (kv cache sometimes as "k v cake"), timestamps approximate.

End of transcript.
